claim: A jet engine does four jobs in order: it takes in air, squeezes it, burns fuel in it, and blows the hot gas out of the back to make thrust (suck, squeeze, burn, blow)
source_quote: Large amounts of surrounding air are continuously brought into the engine inlet. … The compressor acts like many rows of airfoils, with each row producing a small jump in pressure. … In the burner a small amount of fuel is combined with the air and ignited. … The turbine takes some energy out of the hot exhaust, but there is enough energy left over to provide thrust to the jet engine by increasing the velocity through the nozzle.
note: NASA Glenn Research Center, Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics (turbojet). 'Suck, squeeze, burn, blow' is the common mnemonic for these four steps; NASA's own parts page says the same order: inlet, compressor, burner, turbine and nozzle. Quotes re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: In a turbofan such as the F404, a big fan at the front pulls air into the engine
source_quote: In the turbofan engine, the core engine is surrounded by a fan in the front and an additional turbine at the rear. … Some of the incoming air passes through the fan and continues on into the core compressor and then the burner, where it is mixed with fuel and combustion occurs.
note: NASA Glenn (turbofan). The F404 is an afterburning turbofan with a three-stage fan and a seven-stage compressor (GE datasheet AE-44044C 'F404 turbofan engines'; Wikipedia, General Electric F404). Quotes re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The engine takes in a lot of air: the F404-IN20 swallows 153 pounds (about 70 kilograms) of air every second
source_quote: Engine Specifications F404-GE-102/103/402 RM12 F404-IN20 Thrust Class 17,700 lb 18,100 lb 19,000 lb Length 154 in 154 in 154 in Maximum diameter 35 in 35 in 35 in Airflow 146 lb/sec 152 lb/sec 153 lb/sec Pressure Ratio 26:1 27:1 28:1
note: GE Aerospace F404 page; the F404-IN20 (Tejas) is the last column: airflow 153 lb/sec, pressure ratio 28:1, thrust class 19,000 lb. GE's datasheet gives the same in kilograms: 70 kg/sec and 84 kN. NASA says 'Large amounts of surrounding air are continuously brought into the engine inlet.' The VO gives no number; if one is shown, label it 'F404-IN20, GE datasheet'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Compressing air makes it hot and packs it tight: the compressor raises the air's pressure and temperature (bicycle pump = ANALOGY)
source_quote: The compressor does work on the gas and increases the pressure and temperature isentropically to station 3 the compressor exit.
note: NASA Glenn (Brayton cycle). 'Packs it tight' is the plain-words version of higher pressure and density (NASA's gas page: pressure, temperature and density are tied together by the equation of state). The bicycle pump is an analogy: its warmth is mostly the heat of fast compression (with some piston friction), so 'felt the pump get hot' is fair. Label the pump inset ANALOGY. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The compressor is rows of small blades that squeeze the air again and again, step after step (F404-IN20 total squeeze 28 to 1)
source_quote: In the multistage compressor, the pressure is multiplied from row to row (8 stages at 1.2 per stage gives a factor of 4.3).
note: NASA Glenn (compressors); NASA's parts page: 'The compressor and the turbine are composed of many rows of small airfoil shaped blades.' F404-IN20 pressure ratio 28:1 (GE F404 page). A compressor-stage counter on screen can say '7 stages + 3 fan stages (F404)' (Wikipedia, General Electric F404). Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Fuel is sprayed into the hot, squeezed air in the burner and lit; the burning goes on steadily while the engine runs (gas-stove flame = ANALOGY)
source_quote: In the burner a small amount of fuel is combined with the air and ignited.
note: NASA Glenn (turbojet). 'Sprayed': Wikipedia (Combustor) explains fuel injectors 'atomize' the fuel, 'in this context it means to form a fine spray'. 'A flame that never goes out' is plain words for steady combustion: NASA says air is 'continuously brought into the engine inlet' and fuel is burned in the burner. 'Far, far bigger' than a stove flame is an analogy, no number. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The burning gas expands and rushes out of the burner toward the turbine and the nozzle
source_quote: The resulting high temperature exhaust gas is used to turn the power turbine
note: NASA Glenn (burner page). NASA's parts page: 'The hot exhaust then passes through the turbine and out the nozzle.' Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The hot gas passes through the turbine and spins it (like wind spinning a ceiling fan = ANALOGY; NASA says the turbine works like a windmill)
source_quote: The hot exhaust flows through the turbine on its way out of the tailpipe. This spins the turbine, which in turn rotates the drive shaft, which spins the compressor to keep the engine running.
note: NASA Special Projects Laboratory (Turbine Cooling) page. NASA Glenn turbojet page: 'The turbine works like a windmill.' Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The turbine is joined by a shaft to the compressor, so the hot gas spins the turbine, the turbine spins the compressor and the engine keeps itself running
source_quote: In a jet engine we use the energy extracted by the turbine to turn the compressor by linking the compressor and the turbine by the central shaft.
note: NASA Glenn (turbojet); NASA Brayton page: 'Because the turbine and compressor are on the same shaft, the work done on the turbine is exactly equal to the work done by the compressor'. Simplification: a turbofan like the F404 has two shafts (a low-pressure shaft carries the fan, a high-pressure shaft the core compressor); NASA turbofan page calls it a 'two spool engine'. The one-shaft picture is fine for the VO. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The rest of the gas shoots out of the back and pushes the jet forward: thrust follows Newton's third law, action and reaction (balloon let go = ANALOGY)
source_quote: His third law states that for every action (force) in nature there is an equal and opposite reaction. … The motion of a jet engine produces thrust and hot exhaust gases flow out the back of the engine, and a thrusting force is produced in the opposite direction.
note: NASA Glenn Beginner's Guide, Newton's laws of motion. The balloon is a classroom picture of the same law (the air rushing out pushes the balloon the other way); label ANALOGY. Quotes re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The white trail you see behind a high-flying jet is a contrail: water vapour from the exhaust condensing and freezing into ice crystals in cold air
source_quote: Water vapor is already present in the atmosphere, but when the extra vapor from the airplane exhaust rapidly saturates already moist air, the water condenses and freezes into minute ice crystals.
note: NASA Earthdata feature article 'On the Trail of Contrails' (28 Dec 2020). Same page: most commercial jets cruise at 26,000 feet or higher, where it is cold enough for the vapour to freeze. The screenplay's contrail shot should therefore be airliner stock, labelled as stock. The VO says only 'You've seen that trail in the sky'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The turbine sits right behind the flame (downstream of the combustion chamber)
source_quote: The turbine is a fan fixed to the drive shaft downstream from the compressor and combustion chamber.
note: NASA Special Projects Laboratory. NASA Glenn parts page: 'Between the compressor and the turbine flow path is the combustion section or burner'. Rolls-Royce 2018: 'the temperature of the gas flow behind the combustion chamber is 2,000°K (1,700°C)'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The first row of the turbine is where the metal meets the most severe conditions in the engine (replacement wording for L15 'the hottest place in the whole engine')
source_quote: The most severe conditions are met in the first row of the turbine.
note: REPLACES L15 'It's the hottest place in the whole engine.' = WRONG as written. The hottest place is the flame in the combustion chamber, and a fighter's afterburner is hotter than the turbine too. (1) Wikipedia, Afterburner (J57 example, an early engine): the highest temperature in the engine, about 2,040 °C, 'occurs in the combustion chamber'; the gas is diluted 'to bring the gas temperature down to a specific value, known as the Turbine Entry Temperature (TET)' of 850 °C 'which gives the turbine an acceptable life'; the afterburner then reheats the gas to 1,390 °C. (2) NASA-hosted report (Heywood and Mikus, 1973, NTRS 19730017094): 'Nitric oxide forms in the primary zone of gas turbine combustors where the burnt gas composition is close to stoichiometric and gas temperatures are highest.' and the secondary air is mixed in 'to complete combustion of the fuel, and cool the gas stream to the temperature distribution required at turbine inlet.' (3) Wikipedia, Combustor: 'Dilution air is air injected through holes in the liner at the end of the combustion chamber to cool the flue gas before it reaches the turbines.' What IS true: the first turbine row is the hardest place for metal, because the blades face that heat while spinning (Cambridge, above; NASA: blades 'have to endure the stress of high-speed rotation but also the extreme heat flowing from the combustion chamber'). VO fix: 'It's where the metal has the toughest job in the whole engine.' Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Rolls-Royce says its single-crystal turbine blades work in temperatures up to 200 degrees above the melting point of their alloy (on-screen: UP TO 200 °C ABOVE MELTING POINT, [ROLLS-ROYCE 2012])
source_quote: Single crystal turbine blades operate in temperatures up to 200 degrees above the melting point of their alloy
note: Rolls-Royce press release 21 Jun 2012 (primary), attributed in the VO. The release gives no unit; RR 2018 uses °C for the same comparison ('2,000°K (1,700°C), which is actually several hundred degrees hotter than the melting point of the blades'), so °C is consistent. RR's figure is for its large civil (Trent) engines. Same release: 'The single crystal turbine blade is a critical component of the jet engine'. Quote re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Cambridge University: the gas entering the first row of the turbine is at about 1,400 °C (on-screen: GAS ~1,400 °C, [UNIV. OF CAMBRIDGE | 2004])
source_quote: The most severe conditions are met in the first row of the turbine. The entry temperature is around 1400 °C.
note: University of Cambridge, Dept of Materials Science, 'Coatings for high temperature applications :: Materials in the gas turbine' by Thomas Sourmail (c) 2004, a teaching page. It says 'entry temperature' for the first turbine row; it does not use the word 'gas', but turbine entry temperature is the gas temperature (the engineers' standard meaning). The page writes degrees as 'o C'. The figure is a 2004 teaching example: Rolls-Royce 2018 gives 1,700 °C behind the combustor for newer engines, so say 'Cambridge puts it at about'. Add 'Celsius' the first time (L17: 'about fourteen hundred degrees Celsius'). Quote re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Cambridge University: with the cooling and the thermal coat the blade metal is at about 930 °C (on-screen: METAL ~930 °C)
source_quote: Temperatures are kept lower at the surface of the blade because of the cooling system (ceramic surface approaching 1100 °C), and the thermal coat takes another 1-200 °C leading to a metal temperature in the vicinity of 930 °C.
note: Same Cambridge page. 930 °C is the metal temperature WITH the cooling system and the thermal coat, in Cambridge's worked example; the page does not call it a typical or measured average for all engines, so keep 'Cambridge puts numbers on it'. The page prints '1-200' where it almost certainly means 100-200 (its sibling page 'Coatings for turbine blades' says the coat gives 'a drop of 100–300 °C between the gas and metal surface temperatures'). The VO explains cooling and coating in the next lines, so the order works. Quote re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The gap between the gas (about 1,400 °C) and the blade metal (about 930 °C) is about 470 °C (OUR CALCULATION; on-screen: OUR CALCULATION ~470 °C)
source_quote: The entry temperature is around 1400 °C. … leading to a metal temperature in the vicinity of 930 °C.
note: OUR CALCULATION: 1,400 minus 930 = 470 °C, simple subtraction of the two Cambridge figures; say 'roughly four hundred and seventy' as the VO does and tag it [OUR CALCULATION]. Caution for the gauge: do NOT draw the alloy's melting point as 1,400 - 200 = 1,200 °C. Cambridge's 1,400 °C and Rolls-Royce's 'up to 200 above the melting point' come from different engines and years, and no source in hand gives the melting point of the blade alloy, so a melting-point line must be labelled ILLUSTRATIVE. Quotes re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Ordinary metal is made of many small crystals (grains) stuck together, and the boundaries where they meet behave differently from the crystals themselves (brick wall = ANALOGY)
source_quote: A piece of metal used to make a bicycle or a handrail is made of many small crystals or grains. … The grain boundaries formed where the grains meet have distinct properties from the rest of the material.
note: University of Cambridge DoITPoMS teaching package. 'MILLIONS of tiny crystals' in the VO: no source counts them. OUR ESTIMATE: grains of 50 down to 10 micrometres mean roughly 8 million to 1 billion per cubic centimetre, so 'millions' fits a thumb-sized lump of fine-grained metal; but Wikipedia (Grain-boundary strengthening) says the Hall-Petch rule holds for grains from 1 millimetre to 1 micrometre, and 1 millimetre grains mean only about 1,000 per cubic centimetre, which is closer to a cast blade. Safer VO: 'countless tiny crystals' or 'many tiny crystals'. Quotes re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: At high temperature the lines between the crystals are the weak spots: grain boundaries are easy paths for atoms to move along, which lowers the metal's resistance to creep
source_quote: Boundaries are easy diffusion paths and therefore reduce the resistance of the material to creep deformation.
note: University of Cambridge, H. K. D. H. Bhadeshia, Superalloys. 'Weak spots' is the plain-words form of this and is true at high temperature (the VO's context). Same page: the equiaxed-grain blade 'has the worst creep life'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Creep: under heat and a heavy pull the metal slowly stretches, along the grain boundaries in ordinary metal; engineers call it creep
source_quote: creep (sometimes called cold flow) is the tendency of a solid material to undergo slow deformation while subject to persistent mechanical stresses. … Creep is more severe in materials that are subjected to heat for long periods and generally increases as they near their melting point. … In Coble creep the atoms diffuse along grain boundaries to elongate the grains along the stress axis.
note: Wikipedia (Creep (deformation)) for the definition and the Coble-creep mechanism; Cambridge (Bhadeshia, above) for the superalloy case. Wikipedia is a secondary source but the statement is textbook. Quotes re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: A steel spoon left in a flame bends slowly (ANALOGY for creep)
source_quote: Creep deformation generally occurs when a material is stressed at a temperature near its melting point.
note: Analogy, not an engine claim: heat softens metal and a load makes it sag slowly. Label the inset ANALOGY. Wikipedia (Creep): 'The effects of creep deformation generally become noticeable at approximately 35% of the melting point (in Kelvin) for metals'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The best blades are grown as one single crystal, so they have no grain boundaries
source_quote: A single-crystal blade is free from γ/γ grain boundaries. Boundaries are easy diffusion paths and therefore reduce the resistance of the material to creep deformation.
note: University of Cambridge (Bhadeshia). 'The best blades' = the hottest stages of modern engines: Wikipedia (Turbine blade) says single-crystal blades 'are ideal for first and second stage turbine blade applications'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The blade alloy is a nickel superalloy with a rare metal, rhenium, mixed in (about 3 percent in the second generation, 6 percent in the third)
source_quote: The second and third generations contain about 3 wt% and 6 wt% of rhenium respectively. Rhenium is a very expensive addition but leads to an improvement in the creep strength.
note: University of Cambridge (Bhadeshia). Nickel: PIB 26 Apr 2021 says DMRL's blades are made 'using a nickel-based super alloy'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: Rhenium is a rare metal: one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust, and most of it is used in jet-engine superalloys
source_quote: Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in Earth’s continental crust; its estimated average crustal abundance is less than 1 part per billion.
note: US Geological Survey, Professional Paper 1802-P (Critical Mineral Resources of the United States), abstract. Same abstract: 'More than 80 percent of the rhenium consumed in the world is used in high-temperature superalloys, especially those used to make turbine blades for jet aircraft engines.' USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 puts world production at 81,000 kilograms in 2025 (81 tonnes). Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The hot-stage blades are hollow, with channels inside, and cooler air taken from the compressor is pushed through them
source_quote: Air cooling, which diverts excess air flow from the compressor into hollow turbine blades to carry away the heat, is the least expensive type of cooling.
note: NASA Special Projects Laboratory. NASA technology page LEW-TOPS-52: 'cool air is bled from the compressor, ducted to one or more internal chambers of the turbine blades, and discharged through one or more cooling holes to form cooling jets'. 'Cooler' means cooler than the gas, not cold. 'Each blade is hollow' is wider than the sources, which describe the air-cooled hot-stage blades (Wikipedia, Turbine blade, says single-crystal blades 'are ideal for first and second stage turbine blade applications'); none says every blade in the engine is hollow. VO fix: 'These blades are hollow, with tiny channels inside.' Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The cooling air comes out through rows of tiny holes and spreads over the blade as a thin protective layer of cool air (film cooling)
source_quote: Film cooling ejects cooling air from holes in the blade, resulting in a thin layer of cool air on the blade surface.
note: NASA Special Projects Laboratory; NASA technology page LEW-TOPS-52 describes the same 'cooling holes' and 'cooling jets'. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: An air curtain at a shop or mall door is a stream of air blown across the opening to keep two spaces apart (ANALOGY for film cooling)
source_quote: An air door or air curtain is a device used to prevent air, contaminants, or flying insects from moving from one open space to another.
note: Wikipedia (Air door), which quotes ASHRAE's definition. Analogy only: the engine's film hugs the blade surface; an air curtain separates two rooms. Label ANALOGY. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: A thin ceramic coating on the blade has very low thermal conductivity and so slows the heat reaching the metal
source_quote: These are ceramic coatings with very low thermal conductivity. Despite being typically 1/5 mm thin, they allow for a drop of 100–300 °C between the gas and metal surface temperatures.
note: University of Cambridge, 'Coatings for turbine blades' (T. Sourmail). Wikipedia (Thermal barrier coating): these coatings are '100 μm to 2 mm thick' and are usually yttria-stabilised zirconia. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The wall of a thermos flask slows heat because the gap between its two walls is partly emptied of air (ANALOGY for the coating)
source_quote: The gap between the two vessels is partially evacuated of air, creating a partial-vacuum which reduces heat conduction or convection.
note: Wikipedia (Vacuum flask). Analogy only: the coating works by being a poor conductor, not by a vacuum. The VO says 'like the wall of a thermos flask. It slows the heat', which is fair; label ANALOGY. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The blades are cooled inside and outside so the metal stays far below the gas temperature: below the critical material temperature
source_quote: They are therefore cooled both internally and externally in order to keep them below the critical material temperature.
note: Rolls-Royce 'Our stories' (2018). 'Far below the gas' is backed by the Cambridge numbers (about 1,400 °C gas, about 930 °C metal, our gap of about 470 °C). Quote re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: The disc holding the blades turns at more than 12,000 revolutions a minute
source_quote: sit in a disc that rotates at more than 12,000 rpm.
note: Rolls-Royce press release 21 Jun 2012 (its Trent engines). The VO attributes the bus line to Rolls-Royce (L29) but not this one; since both come from the same RR release, say 'Rolls-Royce says' on L28 too, or 'in a big Rolls-Royce engine'. We found no F404 figure. Quote re-matched on the live page 22 Oct 2026.

claim: A rocket engine fires for minutes, not hours, and then its stage falls away (ISRO LVM3: the S200 boosters burn about 134 seconds, the core stage about 200, the upper stage about 646)

claim: A fighter engine has to go from idle to full power in seconds
source_quote: from not more than 15 percent of the rated takeoff power or thrust available to 95 percent rated takeoff power or thrust in not over 5 sec.
note: FAA rule 14 CFR 33.73 quoted in NASA/TM-2009-215668. That is the CIVIL minimum (95 percent in 5 seconds or less); a fighter must respond at least as fast. GE's F404 page says 'The F404 offers unrestricted engine performance on demand with rapid engine throttle response and zero throttle restrictions.' We found no published idle-to-full figure for the F404, so say 'in seconds', not a number. Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.

claim: A rocket is a different job from a fighter engine: a short sprint (rocket) against a long, repeated, controllable run (fighter) (VO: 'Why is a rocket easier?')

note: Narrator's framing; commentary source (Eurasia Review, 28 Feb 2026, citing Swarajya's Raghavan S. Rao). 'Easier' is too strong: a rocket engine is hard in its own ways (ISRO's own upper stage on the same LVM3 page is 'cryogenic stage with 28 tonnes of propellant loading (LOX /LH2)'). Because you only need it for minutes.' Quote re-matched 22 Oct 2026.
